einzeiler: Looking back at summer reading highs, lows, and book club favorites
kurzfassung: The hosts review a wide variety of summer reading picks, ranging from massive epics and divisive novels to acclaimed campus stories and historical fiction. They share personal reading experiences from holidays and bookshop hunts while preparing for the upcoming Booker shortlist. Regular contributor Phil Chafee also joins in to share his favorite recent nonfiction and fiction discoveries.
stichpunkte: Discussion of finishing Robert Caro's massive transportation epic, The Power Broker
Debating the merits and flaws of Alex E. Harrow's time-loop novel, The Everlasting
Mixed reactions to Gwendolyn Riley's bleak contemporary release, The Palm House
Praise for Olivia Laing's beautifully restrained novel set in 1970s Venice, The Silver Book
Exploring Pankaj Mishra's slow-burn coming-of-age novel set in Benares, The Romantics
Reviewing Julia May Jonas's darkly engaging campus novel, Vladimir
Examining Joanna Miller's historical campus novel about early female students at Oxford, The Eights
Phil Chafee sharing thoughts on a biography of Paul Gauguin and Bret Easton Ellis's novel The Shards

beschreibung:
It’s the end of summer, so Kate and Laura are looking back over their holiday reading, the books they loved, the ones that disappointed them, and the unexpected discoveries that made their reading lists longer rather than shorter.
We talk about Alex E. Harrow’s huge fantasy novel The Everlasting, and why it turned out to be a surprisingly divisive read. Kate reports back on her pick from the Booker longlist, The Palm House by Gwendolyn Riley. She's also recently completed The Power Broker, Robert Caro's iconic book on New York master-builder Robert Moses, but was it worth the read? She's also discussing The Silver Book, Olivia Laing's most recent work of fiction. In Pankaj Mishra’s The Romantics, Laura found an interesting book club choice, while Kate's flagging up Vladimir by Julia May Jonas, and while on the campus novel theme she also read Joanna Miller’s The Eights, set in 1920s Oxford. Laura wraps things up with the wonderfully atmospheric The Night Tiger by Yangsze Choo.
But there’s more as pod-regular Phil Chaffee joins us with two of his favourite summer reads, Sue Prideaux’s Wild Thing: A Life of Paul Gauguin and Bret Easton Ellis’s The Shards.
As summer comes to an end, we’re also looking ahead to Booker season, with the shortlist just around the corner and plenty more reading on the horizon.
